claim: The basic reproduction number (R0) for SARS-CoV-2 suggests each infection directly generates 2–4 more infections in the absence of countermeasures like physical distancing.
source: The basic reproduction number, R0, suggests each infection directly generates 2–4 more infections in the absence of countermeasures like physical distancing.
evidence: This claim is supported by epidemiological data and modeling presented in the manuscript, as well as citations to peer-reviewed literature (Li et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020).

claim: The current best-estimate of the median latent time for SARS-CoV-2 is approximately 3 days.
source: The current best-estimate of the median latent time is ≈3 days followed by ≈4 days of close to maximal infectiousness (Li et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed studies (Li et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020) that measured latent periods.

claim: After the latent period, there are approximately 4 days of close to maximal infectiousness for SARS-CoV-2.
source: The current best-estimate of the median latent time is ≈3 days followed by ≈4 days of close to maximal infectiousness (Li et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed studies (Li et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020) that characterized the infectious period.

claim: Using R0≈4, the number of SARS-CoV-2 cases will quadruple every approximately 7 days.
source: Using R0≈4, the number of cases will quadruple every ≈7 days or double every ≈3 days.
evidence: This is a mathematical inference based on the R0 value and the generation time of the virus.

claim: Using R0≈4, the number of SARS-CoV-2 cases will double every approximately 3 days.
source: Using R0≈4, the number of cases will quadruple every ≈7 days or double every ≈3 days.
evidence: This is a mathematical inference based on the R0 value and the generation time of the virus.

claim: 1000-fold growth of SARS-CoV-2 cases (from one case to 10³) requires 10 doublings and takes approximately 30 days or about one month.
source: 1000-fold growth (going from one case to 103) requires 10 doublings since 210 ≈ 103; 3 days × 10 doublings = 30 days, or about one month.
evidence: This is a mathematical calculation based on the doubling time.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 can achieve approximately 1000-fold growth in one month, a million-fold (10⁶) in two months, and a billion-fold (10⁹) in three months without countermeasures.
source: So we expect ≈1000x growth in one month, a million-fold (106) in two months, and a billion fold (109) in three months.
evidence: This is a mathematical extrapolation based on the calculated doubling time and R0 value.

claim: An effective reproduction number (Re) smaller than one will ensure the number of SARS-CoV-2 infections eventually dwindles.
source: An effective reproduction number (Re) smaller than one will ensure the number of infections eventually dwindles.
evidence: This is based on established epidemiological knowledge about disease transmission dynamics.

claim: The median SARS-CoV-2 incubation period is estimated to be roughly 5 days.
source: The median SARS-CoV-2 incubation period is estimated to be roughly 5 days (Lauer et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Lauer et al., 2020).

claim: Approximately 99% of those showing SARS-CoV-2 symptoms will show them before day 14.
source: Approximately 99% of those showing symptoms will show them before day 14, which explains the two week confinement period.
evidence: This is inferred from the incubation period data cited from Lauer et al., 2020.

claim: N95 masks are designed to remove more than 95% of all particles that are at least 0.3 microns (µm) in diameter.
source: N95 masks are designed to remove more than 95% of all particles that are at least 0.3 microns (µm) in diameter.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about N95 mask specifications.

claim: Measurements of the particle filtration efficiency of N95 masks show that they are capable of filtering approximately 99.8% of particles with a diameter of approximately 0.1 μm.
source: In fact, measurements of the particle filtration efficiency of N95 masks show that they are capable of filtering ≈99.8% of particles with a diameter of ≈0.1 μm (Rengasamy et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Rengasamy et al., 2017) that measured mask filtration efficiency.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is an enveloped virus approximately 0.1 μm in diameter.
source: SARS-CoV-2 is an enveloped virus ≈0.1 μm in diameter, so N95 masks are capable of filtering most free virions, but they do more than that.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in the manuscript about viral dimensions.

claim: The characteristic diameter of large respiratory droplets produced by sneezing is approximately 100 μm.
source: The characteristic diameter of large droplets produced by sneezing is ~100 μm (Han et al., 2013), while the diameter of droplet nuclei produced by coughing is on the order of ~1 μm (Yang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed studies (Han et al., 2013).

claim: The diameter of droplet nuclei produced by coughing is on the order of approximately 1 μm.
source: The characteristic diameter of large droplets produced by sneezing is ~100 μm (Han et al., 2013), while the diameter of droplet nuclei produced by coughing is on the order of ~1 μm (Yang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed studies (Yang et al., 2007).

claim: N95 masks should provide some protection against both surface and airborne transmission of SARS-CoV-2.
source: At present, it is unclear whether surfaces or air are the dominant mode of SARS-CoV-2 transmission, but N95 masks should provide some protection against both (Jefferson et al., 2009; Leung et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed studies (Jefferson et al., 2009; Leung et al., 2020) and inference from mask filtration properties.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is a beta-coronavirus whose genome is a single approximately 30 kb strand of RNA.
source: SARS-CoV-2 is a beta-coronavirus whose genome is a single ≈30 kb strand of RNA.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data presented in the manuscript and established knowledge about coronavirus classification.

claim: Flu viruses have smaller genomes (approximately 14 kb) encoded in eight distinct strands of RNA.
source: Flu viruses have smaller genomes (≈14 kb) encoded in eight distinct strands of RNA, and they infect human cells in a different manner than coronaviruses.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about influenza virus structure.

claim: Flu viruses infect human cells in a different manner than coronaviruses.
source: Flu viruses have smaller genomes (≈14 kb) encoded in eight distinct strands of RNA, and they infect human cells in a different manner than coronaviruses.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about viral infection mechanisms.

claim: Cold-causing coronaviruses (e.g. OC43 and 229E strains) are quite similar to SARS-CoV-2 in genome length (within 10%).
source: Cold-causing coronaviruses (e.g. OC43 and 229E strains) are quite similar to SARS-CoV-2 in genome length (within 10%) and gene content, but different from SARS-CoV-2 in sequence (≈50% nucleotide identity) and infection severity.
evidence: This is supported by genomic comparison data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cold-causing coronaviruses (e.g. OC43 and 229E strains) are quite similar to SARS-CoV-2 in gene content.
source: Cold-causing coronaviruses (e.g. OC43 and 229E strains) are quite similar to SARS-CoV-2 in genome length (within 10%) and gene content, but different from SARS-CoV-2 in sequence (≈50% nucleotide identity) and infection severity.
evidence: This is supported by genomic comparison data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cold-causing coronaviruses (e.g. OC43 and 229E strains) are different from SARS-CoV-2 in sequence (approximately 50% nucleotide identity).
source: Cold-causing coronaviruses (e.g. OC43 and 229E strains) are quite similar to SARS-CoV-2 in genome length (within 10%) and gene content, but different from SARS-CoV-2 in sequence (≈50% nucleotide identity) and infection severity.
evidence: This is supported by genomic comparison data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cold-causing coronaviruses (e.g. OC43 and 229E strains) are different from SARS-CoV-2 in infection severity.
source: Cold-causing coronaviruses (e.g. OC43 and 229E strains) are quite similar to SARS-CoV-2 in genome length (within 10%) and gene content, but different from SARS-CoV-2 in sequence (≈50% nucleotide identity) and infection severity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about disease severity differences between common cold and COVID-19.

claim: Coronaviruses have the largest genomes of any known RNA viruses (approximately 30 kb).
source: One interesting facet of coronaviruses is that they have the largest genomes of any known RNA viruses (≈30 kb).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about RNA virus genome sizes.

claim: Coronaviruses have a proofreading exonuclease called ExoN.
source: Indeed, coronaviruses have a proofreading exonuclease called ExoN, which explains their low mutation rates (~10–6 per site per cycle) in comparison to influenza (≈3 × 10–5 per site per cycle; Sanjuán et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about coronavirus molecular biology.

claim: Coronaviruses have low mutation rates (~10⁻⁶ per site per cycle) in comparison to influenza (≈3 × 10⁻⁵ per site per cycle).
source: Indeed, coronaviruses have a proofreading exonuclease called ExoN, which explains their low mutation rates (~10–6 per site per cycle) in comparison to influenza (≈3 × 10–5 per site per cycle; Sanjuán et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Sanjuán et al., 2010) that measured mutation rates.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has a single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome that codes for 10 genes ultimately producing 26 proteins according to an NCBI annotation.
source: SARS-CoV-2 has a single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome that codes for 10 genes ultimately producing 26 proteins according to an NCBI annotation (NC_045512).
evidence: This is supported by genomic annotation data from NCBI.

claim: One long SARS-CoV-2 gene, orf1ab, encodes a polyprotein that is cleaved into 16 proteins by proteases that are themselves part of the polyprotein.
source: One long gene, orf1ab, encodes a polyprotein that is cleaved into 16 proteins by proteases that are themselves part of the polyprotein.
evidence: This is supported by genomic and proteomic data about SARS-CoV-2.

claim: It is currently possible to ascribe clear biochemical or structural functions to only about half of SARS-CoV-2 gene products.
source: Though much current work is centered on understanding the role of 'accessory' proteins in the viral life cycle, we estimate that it is currently possible to ascribe clear biochemical or structural functions to only about half of SARS-CoV-2 gene products.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current state of knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 proteins.

claim: The evolutionary rate is defined as the average number of substitutions that become fixed per year in strains of the virus, given in units of mutations per site per year.
source: The first is the evolutionary rate, which is defined as the average number of substitutions that become fixed per year in strains of the virus, given in units of mutations per site per year.
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge in evolutionary biology.

claim: The mutation rate is the number of substitutions per site per replication cycle.
source: The second is the mutation rate, which is the number of substitutions per site per replication cycle.
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge in virology.

claim: A single site in a β-coronavirus genome will accumulate approximately 10⁻⁶ mutations in each round of replication.
source: The only measurement of a mutation rate in a β-coronavirus suggests that this site will accumulate ~10–6 mutations in each round of replication.
evidence: This is based on mutation rate measurements in β-coronaviruses.

claim: Each coronavirus replication cycle takes approximately 10 hours.
source: Each replication cycle takes ~10 hr, and so there are 103 cycles/year.
evidence: This is based on data about coronavirus replication kinetics presented in the manuscript.

claim: There are approximately 10³ coronavirus replication cycles per year.
source: Each replication cycle takes ~10 hr, and so there are 103 cycles/year.
evidence: This is a mathematical calculation based on the replication cycle duration.

claim: The virus undergoes near-continuous replication in the wild, constantly generating new mutations that accumulate over the course of the year.
source: As our estimate is consistent with the measured rate, we infer that the virus undergoes near-continuous replication in the wild, constantly generating new mutations that accumulate over the course of the year.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency between calculated and measured evolutionary rates.

claim: Since the mutation rate is approximately 10⁻⁶ mutations/site/cycle and an mL of sputum might contain upwards of 10⁷ viral RNAs, every site is mutated more than once in such samples.
source: For example, since the mutation rate is ~10–6 mutations/site/cycle and an mL of sputum might contain upwards of 107 viral RNAs, we infer that every site is mutated more than once in such samples.
evidence: This is a mathematical inference based on mutation rate and viral load data.

claim: The number of infectious SARS-CoV-2 virions is typically much lower than inferred from measurements of the viral genome.
source: The number of infectious virions is typically much lower than inferred from measurements of the viral genome (Woelfel et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Woelfel et al., 2020).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 RNA has been detected on various surfaces several weeks after they were last touched.
source: SARS-CoV-2 RNA has been detected on various surfaces several weeks after they were last touched (Moriarty et al., 2020), but infectiousness appears to degrade more quickly than RNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study (Moriarty et al., 2020).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infectiousness appears to degrade more quickly than RNA on surfaces.
source: SARS-CoV-2 RNA has been detected on various surfaces several weeks after they were last touched (Moriarty et al., 2020), but infectiousness appears to degrade more quickly than RNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing RNA detection and infectivity measurements.

claim: The stability of infectious SARS-CoV-2 virions on plastic is much greater than on copper or steel.
source: When researchers measured the stability of infectious virions on surfaces, the numbers depended greatly on the type of surface and the medium carrying the virus, with the stability on plastic being much greater than on copper or steel, for example.
evidence: This is based on data from viral stability studies.

claim: Viral stability is known to depend strongly on temperature and humidity.
source: Viral stability is also known to depend strongly on temperature and humidity (Chin et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Chin et al., 2020).

claim: The basic reproduction number R0 estimates the average number of new infections directly generated by a single infectious person.
source: The basic reproduction number, R0, estimates the average number of new infections directly generated by a single infectious person.
evidence: This is a definition based on established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: The 0 subscript in R0 connotes that this refers to early stages of an epidemic, when everyone in the region is susceptible and no countermeasures have been taken.
source: The 0 subscript connotes that this refers to early stages of an epidemic, when everyone in the region is susceptible (that is, there is no immunity) and no countermeasures have been taken.
evidence: This is a definition based on established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Estimates of R0 can vary between locales because geography and culture affect how many people we encounter daily, how much we touch them and share food with them.
source: As geography and culture affect how many people we encounter daily, how much we touch them and share food with them, estimates of R0 can vary between locales.
evidence: This is based on epidemiological knowledge about factors affecting disease transmission.

claim: Several days pass before a newly-infected person becomes infectious themselves, a period called the 'latent period'.
source: Several days pass before a newly-infected person becomes infectious themselves. This 'latent period' is typically followed by several days of infectivity called the 'infectious period'.
evidence: This is a definition based on established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: The latent period is typically followed by several days of infectivity called the 'infectious period'.
source: Several days pass before a newly-infected person becomes infectious themselves. This 'latent period' is typically followed by several days of infectivity called the 'infectious period'.
evidence: This is a definition based on established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Viral RNA was detectable in patients with moderate SARS-CoV-2 symptoms for more than one week after the onset of symptoms.
source: For example, viral RNA was detectable in patients with moderate symptoms for more than one week after the onset of symptoms, and more than two weeks in patients with severe symptoms (ECDC, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to ECDC data (ECDC, 2020).

claim: Viral RNA was detectable in patients with severe SARS-CoV-2 symptoms for more than two weeks after the onset of symptoms.
source: For example, viral RNA was detectable in patients with moderate symptoms for more than one week after the onset of symptoms, and more than two weeks in patients with severe symptoms (ECDC, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to ECDC data (ECDC, 2020).

claim: Direct measurement of latent and infectious periods at the individual level is extremely challenging, as accurately identifying the precise time of infection is usually very difficult.
source: Direct measurement of latent and infectious periods at the individual level is extremely challenging, as accurately identifying the precise time of infection is usually very difficult.
evidence: This is based on knowledge about the practical challenges of epidemiological measurements.

claim: Quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) measures the number of copies of viral RNA in a sample.
source: One common approach is to quantify the amount of viral RNA in an environmental (e.g., surface) or clinical (e.g., sputum) sample via quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). This method measures the number of copies of viral RNA in a sample.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about RT-qPCR methodology.

claim: The presence of viral RNA does not necessarily imply the presence of infectious virions.
source: The presence of viral RNA does not necessarily imply the presence of infectious virions.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the difference between RNA detection and infectivity.

claim: Measuring TCID50 involves infecting replicate cultures of susceptible cells with dilutions of the virus and noting the dilution at which half the replicate dishes become infected.
source: Measuring TCID50 involves infecting replicate cultures of susceptible cells with dilutions of the virus and noting the dilution at which half the replicate dishes become infected.
evidence: This is a description of the TCID50 methodology based on established virological knowledge.

claim: Viral counts reported by TCID50 tend to be much lower than RT-qPCR measurements.
source: Viral counts reported by TCID50 tend to be much lower than RT-qPCR measurements, which could be one reason why studies relying on RNA measurements (Moriarty et al., 2020) report the persistence of viral RNA on surfaces for much longer times than studies relying on TCID50 (van Doremalen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing different measurement methodologies and their results from cited studies.

claim: For the common cold, approximately 0.1 TCID50 are sufficient to infect half of the people exposed.
source: Nevertheless, for many viruses even a small dose of virions can lead to infection. For the common cold, for example, ~0.1 TCID50 are sufficient to infect half of the people exposed (Couch et al., 1966).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Couch et al., 1966).

claim: The case fatality rate (CFR) is the proportion of fatalities out of total diagnosed cases.
source: One commonly reported measure is the case fatality rate (CFR), which is the proportion of fatalities out of total diagnosed cases.
evidence: This is a definition based on established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: The CFR reported in different countries varies significantly, from 1% to about 15%.
source: The CFR reported in different countries varies significantly, from 1% to about 15%.
evidence: This is based on epidemiological data from different countries.

claim: The majority of people dying from SARS-CoV-2 have a preexisting condition such as cardiovascular disease or smoking.
source: For example, the prevalence of smoking, the average age of the population, and the capacity of the healthcare system. Indeed, the majority of people dying from SARS-CoV-2 have a preexisting condition such as cardiovascular disease or smoking (The Novel Coronavirus Pneumonia Emergency Response Epidemiology Team, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an epidemiological report (The Novel Coronavirus Pneumonia Emergency Response Epidemiology Team, 2020).

claim: The CFR will tend to overestimate the rate of fatalities per infected person because many cases with mild or no symptoms are not tested.
source: Even when correcting for these factors, the CFR does not give a complete picture as many cases with mild or no symptoms are not tested. Thus, the CFR will tend to overestimate the rate of fatalities per infected person, termed the infection fatality rate (IFR).
evidence: This is an inference based on epidemiological knowledge about testing biases.

claim: The infection fatality rate (IFR) is the rate of fatalities per infected person.
source: Thus, the CFR will tend to overestimate the rate of fatalities per infected person, termed the infection fatality rate (IFR).
evidence: This is a definition based on established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 does not release its progeny by lysing the cell, but rather by continuous budding.
source: SARS-CoV-2 does not release its progeny by lysing the cell, but rather by continuous budding (Park et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Park et al., 2020b).

claim: The eclipse period is the lag between inoculation and the appearance of new intracellular virions.
source: Assuming entry of the virus to the cells is rapid (we estimate 10 min for SARS-CoV-2), the time it takes to produce progeny can be estimated by quantifying the lag between inoculation and the appearance of new intracellular virions, also known as the 'eclipse period'.
evidence: This is a definition based on established virological knowledge.

claim: The latent period (in virology) is the time from cell entry until the appearance of the first extracellular viruses.
source: The time from cell entry until the appearance of the first extracellular viruses, known as the 'latent period' (not to be confused with the epidemiological latent period; see glossary in Box 1), estimates the duration of the full replication cycle.
evidence: This is a definition based on established virological knowledge.

claim: For the seasonal flu, most transmissions occur after a person has developed symptoms.
source: For the seasonal flu, for example, most transmissions indeed occur after a person has developed symptoms (Ip et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Ip et al., 2017).

claim: For SARS-CoV-2, it is common to be contagious before symptoms.
source: For SARS-CoV-2, in contrast, it is common to be contagious before symptoms.
evidence: This is supported by data about SARS-CoV-2 transmission dynamics.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 incubation period is about 5 days.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 incubation period is about 5 days, while peak infectiousness begins two days before symptoms reveal themselves.
evidence: This is supported by epidemiological data cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Peak SARS-CoV-2 infectiousness begins two days before symptoms reveal themselves.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 incubation period is about 5 days, while peak infectiousness begins two days before symptoms reveal themselves.
evidence: This is supported by epidemiological data about SARS-CoV-2 transmission.

claim: A large fraction of SARS-CoV-2 infections occur pre-symptomatically.
source: As a result, a large fraction of infections occur pre-symptomatically, that is, without the infectious person realizing they have the disease (Ferretti et al., 2020; He et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed studies (Ferretti et al., 2020; He et al., 2020).

claim: Diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 typically occurs approximately 5 days after symptom onset, or approximately 10 days after infection.
source: With testing capacity under strain, diagnosis typically occurs ≈5 days after symptom onset, or ≈10 days after infection.
evidence: This is based on data about testing timelines.

claim: By the time of diagnosis, most SARS-CoV-2 infected people have already passed peak infectiousness.
source: By that time, most people have already passed peak infectiousness.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of peak infectiousness and diagnosis.

claim: There is strong evidence of significant pre-symptomatic transmission of SARS-CoV-2.
source: In the case of SARS-CoV-2 this means detection before symptoms because there is strong evidence of significant pre-symptomatic transmission.
evidence: This is supported by epidemiological data cited in the manuscript.

claim: A large fraction of SARS-CoV-2 cases are asymptomatic, meaning the infected person never develops noticeable symptoms.
source: Finally, the situation is further complicated by a large fraction of asymptomatic cases, that is cases in which the infected person never develops noticeable symptoms.
evidence: This is based on epidemiological observations of SARS-CoV-2 infections.

claim: More than half of children and young adults with SARS-CoV-2 are asymptomatic.
source: This fraction is more than half of children and young adults (Davies et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Davies et al., 2020).

claim: Leading modeling efforts assume that asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infections are anywhere between 10–80% as contagious as symptomatic ones.
source: Leading modeling efforts assume that asymptomatic infections are anywhere between 10–80% as contagious as symptomatic ones (Ferretti et al., 2020; Davies et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling studies (Ferretti et al., 2020; Davies et al., 2020).

claim: The diameter of SARS-CoV-2 varies from about 60 to 140 nm.
source: Diameter. (Figure 3 in Zhu et al., 2020): "Electron micrographs of negative-stained 2019-nCoV particles were generally spherical with some pleomorphism. Diameter varied from about 60 to 140 nm."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to electron microscopy data (Zhu et al., 2020).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 particles are generally spherical with some pleomorphism.
source: Diameter. (Figure 3 in Zhu et al., 2020): "Electron micrographs of negative-stained 2019-nCoV particles were generally spherical with some pleomorphism. Diameter varied from about 60 to 140 nm."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to electron microscopy data (Zhu et al., 2020).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has approximately 90 spike trimers per particle.
source: Number of spike trimers. (Neuman et al., 2011): "Our model predicts ∼90 spikes per particle."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a modeling study (Neuman et al., 2011).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 spike trimers are about 9 to 12 nm in length.
source: Length of spike trimers. (Zhu et al., 2020): "Virus particles had quite distinctive spikes, about 9 to 12 nm, and gave virions the appearance of a solar corona."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to electron microscopy data (Zhu et al., 2020).

claim: Walls et al., 2020 reports a receptor binding affinity (Kd) of approximately 1 nM for the SARS-CoV-2 binding domain.
source: Receptor binding affinity (Kd). Walls et al., 2020 reports Kd of ≈1 nM for the binding domain using biolayer interferometry with kon of ≈1.5 × 105 M–1 s–1 and koff of ≈1.6 × 10–4 s–1 (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Walls et al., 2020) with specific binding kinetics data.

claim: Wrapp et al., 2020 reports a receptor binding affinity (Kd) of approximately 15 nM for the SARS-CoV-2 spike.
source: Wrapp et al., 2020 reports Kd of ≈15 nM for the spike (Figure 3) and ≈35 nM for the binding domain (Figure 4) using surface plasmon resonance with kon of ≈1.9 × 105 M–1 s–1 and koff of ≈2.8 × 10–3 s–1 for the spike, and kon of ≈1.4 × 105 M–1 s–1 and koff of ≈4.7 × 10–3 s–1 for the binding domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Wrapp et al., 2020) with specific binding kinetics data.

claim: Wrapp et al., 2020 reports a receptor binding affinity (Kd) of approximately 35 nM for the SARS-CoV-2 binding domain.
source: Wrapp et al., 2020 reports Kd of ≈15 nM for the spike (Figure 3) and ≈35 nM for the binding domain (Figure 4) using surface plasmon resonance with kon of ≈1.9 × 105 M–1 s–1 and koff of ≈2.8 × 10–3 s–1 for the spike, and kon of ≈1.4 × 105 M–1 s–1 and koff of ≈4.7 × 10–3 s–1 for the binding domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Wrapp et al., 2020) with specific binding kinetics data.

claim: Lan et al., 2020 reports a receptor binding affinity (Kd) of approximately 5 nM for the SARS-CoV-2 binding domain.
source: Lan et al., 2020 reports Kd of ≈5 nM for the binding domain (Extended Data Figure 4) using surface plasmon resonance with kon of ≈1.4 × 106 M–1 s–1 and koff of ≈6.5 × 10–3 s–1.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Lan et al., 2020) with specific binding kinetics data.

claim: Shang et al., 2020 reports a receptor binding affinity (Kd) of approximately 40 nM for the SARS-CoV-2 binding domain.
source: Shang et al., 2020 reports Kd of ≈40 nM for the binding domain (Extended Data Figure 6) using surface plasmon resonance with kon of ≈1.8 × 106 M–1 s–1 and koff of ≈7.8 × 10–3 s–1.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Shang et al., 2020) with specific binding kinetics data.

claim: The main disagreement between receptor binding affinity studies seems to be on the koff (dissociation rate constant).
source: The main disagreement between the studies seems to be on the koff.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the kinetic parameters reported in multiple studies.

claim: An average SARS-CoV particle contains approximately 1100 M2 (membrane protein) molecules.
source: Membrane (M; 222 aa). (Neuman et al., 2011): "Using the M spacing data for each virus (Figure 6C), this would give ∼1100 M2 molecules per average SARS-CoV, MHV and FCoV particle."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a structural study (Neuman et al., 2011).

claim: Approximately 15–30 copies of envelope protein are incorporated into TGEV virions.
source: Envelope (E; 75 aa). (Godet et al., 1992): "Based on the estimated molar ratio and assuming that coronavirions bear 100 (J Gen Virol 63: 241–245) to 200 spikes, each composed of 3 s molecules (Virus Research 20:107–120) it can be inferred that approximately 15–30 copies of ORF4 protein are incorporated into TGEV virions (Purdue strain)."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on TGEV coronavirus (Godet et al., 1992).

claim: Estimated ratios of M to N protein in purified coronaviruses range from about 3M:1N to 1M:1N, giving 730–2200 N molecules per virion.
source: Nucleoprotein (364 aa). (Neuman et al., 2011): "Estimated ratios of M to N protein in purified coronaviruses range from about 3M:1N (Cavanagh, 1983; Escors et al., 2001) to 1M:1N (Hogue and Brian, 1986; Liu and Inglis, 1991), giving 730–2200 N molecules per virion."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review (Neuman et al., 2011) that cites multiple earlier studies.

claim: The initial isolate of SARS-CoV-2 from Wuhan, China has a 29903 nt ≈ 30 kb ssRNA genome.
source: Genome length. The initial isolate of SARS-CoV-2 from Wuhan, China has a 29903 nt ≈ 30 kb ssRNA genome (NCBI MN908947.3), which is typical of a coronavirus (Smith and Denison, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence data from NCBI and a citation to a review (Smith and Denison, 2012).

claim: A 29903 nt ≈ 30 kb ssRNA genome is typical of a coronavirus.
source: Genome length. The initial isolate of SARS-CoV-2 from Wuhan, China has a 29903 nt ≈ 30 kb ssRNA genome (NCBI MN908947.3), which is typical of a coronavirus (Smith and Denison, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review (Smith and Denison, 2012) about coronavirus genomes.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 genome has 10 open reading frames.
source: (Wu et al., 2020b): "SARS-CoV-2 genome has 10 open reading frames (Figure 2A)".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a genomic analysis study (Wu et al., 2020b).

claim: Mutation rates estimated for SARS, MERS, and OC43 show a large range, covering a span of 0.27 to 2.38 substitutions × 10⁻³/site/year.
source: Evolution rate. (Koyama et al., 2020): "Mutation rates estimated for SARS, MERS, and OC43 show a large range, covering a span of 0.27 to 2.38 substitutions × 10–3/site/ year (see references 10–16)."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review (Koyama et al., 2020) that summarizes multiple studies.

claim: The corrected estimate of the mutation rate for murine hepatitis virus is 3.5 × 10⁻⁶ per site per cycle.
source: Mutation rate. (Sanjuán et al., 2010): "Murine hepatitis virus … Therefore, the corrected estimate of the mutation rate is μs/n/c = 1.9x10–6 / 0.55 = 3.5 x 10–6."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a peer-reviewed study (Sanjuán et al., 2010) that measured mutation rates.

claim: Bat coronavirus RaTG13 has 96% nucleotide sequence identity to SARS-CoV-2.
source: Genomes used: bat coronavirus RaTG13 (MN996532.1; 96% id); SARS-CoV-1 (NC_004718.3; 80% id); MERS (NC_019843.3; 55% id); human cold coronavirus strains OC43 (NC_006213.1; 53% id) and 229E (NC_002645.1; 50% id).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence alignment data from NCBI.

claim: SARS-CoV-1 has 80% nucleotide sequence identity to SARS-CoV-2.
source: Genomes used: bat coronavirus RaTG13 (MN996532.1; 96% id); SARS-CoV-1 (NC_004718.3; 80% id); MERS (NC_019843.3; 55% id); human cold coronavirus strains OC43 (NC_006213.1; 53% id) and 229E (NC_002645.1; 50% id).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence alignment data from NCBI.

claim: MERS has 55% nucleotide sequence identity to SARS-CoV-2.
source: Genomes used: bat coronavirus RaTG13 (MN996532.1; 96% id); SARS-CoV-1 (NC_004718.3; 80% id); MERS (NC_019843.3; 55% id); human cold coronavirus strains OC43 (NC_006213.1; 53% id) and 229E (NC_002645.1; 50% id).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence alignment data from NCBI.

claim: Human cold coronavirus strain OC43 has 53% nucleotide sequence identity to SARS-CoV-2.
source: Genomes used: bat coronavirus RaTG13 (MN996532.1; 96% id); SARS-CoV-1 (NC_004718.3; 80% id); MERS (NC_019843.3; 55% id); human cold coronavirus strains OC43 (NC_006213.1; 53% id) and 229E (NC_002645.1; 50% id).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence alignment data from NCBI.

claim: Human cold coronavirus strain 229E has 50% nucleotide sequence identity to SARS-CoV-2.
source: Genomes used: bat coronavirus RaTG13 (MN996532.1; 96% id); SARS-CoV-1 (NC_004718.3; 80% id); MERS (NC_019843.3; 55% id); human cold coronavirus strains OC43 (NC_006213.1; 53% id) and 229E (NC_002645.1; 50% id).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence alignment data from NCBI.

claim: PangolinCoV is 91.02% identical to SARS-CoV-2 at the whole genome level.
source: For pangolin: '"PangolinCoV is 91.02% and 90.55% identical to SARS-CoV-2 and BatCoV RaTG13, respectively, at the whole genome level" (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a genomic analysis study (Zhang et al., 2020).

claim: PangolinCoV is 90.55% identical to BatCoV RaTG13 at the whole genome level.
source: For pangolin: '"PangolinCoV is 91.02% and 90.55% identical to SARS-CoV-2 and BatCoV RaTG13, respectively, at the whole genome level" (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a genomic analysis study (Zhang et al., 2020).

claim: SARS-CoV-1 virus is internalized within 15 minutes.
source: Virion entry into cell (for SARS-CoV-1). (Schneider et al., 2012): "Previous experiments had revealed that virus is internalized within 15 min".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on SARS-CoV-1 (Schneider et al., 2012).

claim: Within the first 10 minutes of SARS-CoV-1 infection, some virus particles are internalized into vacuoles just below the plasma membrane surface.
source: (Ng et al., 2003): "Within the first 10 min, some virus particles were internalized into vacuoles (arrow) that were just below the plasma membrane surface (Fig. 2, arrows). […] The observation at 15 min postinfection (p.i.), did not differ much from 10 min p.i. (Fig. 4a)".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a microscopy study (Ng et al., 2003).

claim: SARS-CoV replication cycle from adsorption to release of infectious progeny takes about 7 to 8 hours.
source: Eclipse period. (Schneider et al., 2012): "SARS-CoV replication cycle from adsorption to release of infectious progeny takes about 7 to 8 hr (data not shown)";
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on SARS-CoV (Schneider et al., 2012).

claim: The average per-cell yield of active MHV virus was estimated to be about 6–7 × 10² plaque-forming units.
source: Burst size. (Hirano et al., 1976): "The average per-cell yield of active virus was estimated to be about 6–7 × 102 plaque-forming units."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on MHV coronavirus (Hirano et al., 1976).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infects various respiratory epithelial cells, predominantly type II pneumocytes, and alveolar macrophages in the lung.
source: Type. (Shieh et al., 2005): "Immunohistochemical and in situ hybridization assays demonstrated evidence of SARS-associated coronavirus (SARS-CoV) infection in various respiratory epithelial cells, predominantly type II pneumocytes, and in alveolar macrophages in the lung".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a histopathology study (Shieh et al., 2005).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 uses ACE2 to enter target cells.
source: (Walls et al., 2020): "SARS-CoV-2 uses ACE2 to enter target cells".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a molecular biology study (Walls et al., 2020).

claim: In SARS-CoV-2-infected macaques, virus was detected in type I and II pneumocytes in foci of diffuse alveolar damage and mucous glands of the nasal cavity.
source: (Rockx et al., 2020): "In SARS-CoV-2-infected macaques, virus was excreted from nose and throat in absence of clinical signs, and detected in type I and II pneumocytes in foci of diffuse alveolar damage and mucous glands of the nasal cavity […] In the upper respiratory tract, there was focal five or locally extensive SARS-CoV-2 antigen expression in epithelial cells of mucous glands in the nasal cavity (septum or concha) of all four macaques, without any associated histological lesions (fig. 2I)."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an animal model study (Rockx et al., 2020).

claim: In SARS-CoV-2-infected macaques, virus was excreted from nose and throat in absence of clinical signs.
source: (Rockx et al., 2020): "In SARS-CoV-2-infected macaques, virus was excreted from nose and throat in absence of clinical signs, and detected in type I and II pneumocytes in foci of diffuse alveolar damage and mucous glands of the nasal cavity […] In the upper respiratory tract, there was focal five or locally extensive SARS-CoV-2 antigen expression in epithelial cells of mucous glands in the nasal cavity (septum or concha) of all four macaques, without any associated histological lesions (fig. 2I)."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an animal model study (Rockx et al., 2020).

claim: Type II pneumocytes have an estimated mean volume of 763 ± 64 μm³.
source: Type II pneumocyte volume. (Fehrenbach et al., 1995): "Morphometry revealed that although inter-individual variation due to some oedematous swelling was present, the cells were in a normal size range as indicated by an estimated mean volume of 763 ± 64 μm3."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a morphometry study (Fehrenbach et al., 1995).

claim: Alveolar macrophages have a mean volume of 2,491 μm³.
source: Alveolar macrophage volume. (Crapo et al., 1982): "Alveolar macrophages were found to be the largest cell in the populations studied, having a mean volume of 2,491 μm3."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a morphometry study (Crapo et al., 1982).

claim: Alveolar macrophages are the largest cell in the lung cell populations studied.
source: Alveolar macrophage volume. (Crapo et al., 1982): "Alveolar macrophages were found to be the largest cell in the populations studied, having a mean volume of 2,491 μm3."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a morphometry study (Crapo et al., 1982).

claim: The seroconversion for SARS-CoV-2 antibodies sequentially appeared for Ab, IgM and then IgG, with a median time of 11, 12 and 14 days, respectively.
source: Seroconversion time (time period until a specific antibody becomes detectable in the blood). (Zhao et al., 2020): "The seroconversion sequentially appeared for Ab, IgM and then IgG, with a median time of 11, 12 and 14 days, respectively".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a serological study (Zhao et al., 2020).

claim: For 16 patients with serum samples available 14 days or longer after symptom onset, rates of seropositivity were 94% for anti-NP IgG, 88% for anti-NP IgM, 100% for anti-RBD IgG, and 94% for anti-RBD IgM.
source: (To et al., 2020): "For 16 patients with serum samples available 14 days or longer after symptom onset, rates of seropositivity were 94% for anti-NP IgG (n = 15), 88% for anti-NP IgM (n = 14), 100% for anti-RBD IgG (n = 16), and 94% for anti-RBD IgM (n = 15)".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a serological study (To et al., 2020).

claim: Among 176 patients who had SARS, SARS-specific antibodies were maintained for an average of 2 years, and significant reduction of immunoglobulin G–positive percentage and titers occurred in the third year.
source: Maintenance of antibody response to virus. (Wu et al., 2007): "Among 176 patients who had had severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), SARS-specific antibodies were maintained for an average of 2 years, and significant reduction of immunoglobulin G–positive percentage and titers occurred in the third year".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a longitudinal serological study (Wu et al., 2007).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 RNA was identified on a variety of surfaces in cabins of both symptomatic and asymptomatic infected passengers up to 17 days after cabins were vacated on the Diamond Princess but before disinfection procedures had been conducted.
source: RNA stability on surfaces (Moriarty et al., 2020): "SARS-CoV-2 RNA was identified on a variety of surfaces in cabins of both symptomatic and asymptomatic infected passengers up to 17 days after cabins were vacated on the Diamond Princess but before disinfection procedures had been conducted (Takuya Yamagishi, National Institute of Infectious Diseases, personal communication, 2020)."
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a report (Moriarty et al., 2020) that includes personal communication data.

claim: The median estimate of the effective reproductive number (Re) for SARS-CoV-2 is 2.38 (95% CI: 2.04–2.77).
source: Basic reproductive number, R0. (Li et al., 2020a): "Our median estimate of the effective reproductive number, Re – equivalent to the basic reproductive number (R0) at the beginning of the epidemic – is 2.38 (95% CI: 2.04–2.77)".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an epidemiological modeling study (Li et al., 2020a).

claim: The estimated R0 from the pooled distribution has a median of 2.9 (95% CI: 2.1–4.5).
source: (Park et al., 2020a): "Our estimated R0 from the pooled distribution has a median of 2.9 (95% CI: 2.1–4.5)".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an epidemiological modeling study (Park et al., 2020a).

claim: The median estimates for the latent and infectious periods of SARS-CoV-2 are approximately 3.69 and 3.48 days, respectively.
source: Latent period (from infection to being able to transmit). (Li et al., 2020a): "In addition, the median estimates for the latent and infectious periods are approximately 3.69 and 3.48 days, respectively"; see also table 1 in this paper.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an epidemiological modeling study (Li et al., 2020a).

claim: The median incubation period for SARS-CoV-2 was estimated to be 5.1 days (95% CI, 4.5 to 5.8 days).
source: Incubation period (from infection to symptoms). (Lauer et al., 2020): "The median incubation period was estimated to be 5.1 days (95% CI, 4.5 to 5.8 days), and 97.5% of those who develop symptoms will do so within 11.5 days (CI, 8.2 to 15.6 days) of infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an epidemiological study (Lauer et al., 2020).

claim: 97.5% of those who develop SARS-CoV-2 symptoms will do so within 11.5 days (CI, 8.2 to 15.6 days) of infection.
source: (Lauer et al., 2020): "The median incubation period was estimated to be 5.1 days (95% CI, 4.5 to 5.8 days), and 97.5% of those who develop symptoms will do so within 11.5 days (CI, 8.2 to 15.6 days) of infection. These estimates imply that, under conservative assumptions, 101 out of every 10 000 cases (99th percentile, 482) will develop symptoms after 14 days of active monitoring or quarantine".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an epidemiological study (Lauer et al., 2020).

claim: Under conservative assumptions, 101 out of every 10,000 SARS-CoV-2 cases (99th percentile, 482) will develop symptoms after 14 days of active monitoring or quarantine.
source: These estimates imply that, under conservative assumptions, 101 out of every 10 000 cases (99th percentile, 482) will develop symptoms after 14 days of active monitoring or quarantine".
evidence: This is an inference based on the incubation period distribution from Lauer et al., 2020.

claim: The mean incubation period for SARS-CoV-2 was 5.2 days (95% confidence interval [CI], 4.1 to 7.0), with the 95th percentile of the distribution at 12.5 days.
source: (Li et al., 2020b): "The mean incubation period was 5.2 days (95% confidence interval [CI], 4.1 to 7.0), with the 95th percentile of the distribution at 12.5 days".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an epidemiological study (Li et al., 2020b).

claim: The median time from onset to clinical recovery for mild COVID-19 cases is approximately 2 weeks.
source: Disease duration. (WHO, 2020): "Using available preliminary data, the median time from onset to clinical recovery for mild cases is approximately 2 weeks and is 3–6 weeks for patients with severe or critical disease".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO data (WHO, 2020).

claim: The median time from onset to clinical recovery for patients with severe or critical COVID-19 disease is 3–6 weeks.
source: Disease duration. (WHO, 2020): "Using available preliminary data, the median time from onset to clinical recovery for mild cases is approximately 2 weeks and is 3–6 weeks for patients with severe or critical disease".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO data (WHO, 2020).

claim: The overall IFR estimate for China is 0.66% (0.39%, 1.33%).
source: Infection fatality rate. We rely on three independent approaches that estimate the IFR. The first relies on data about people who were extensively tested as a result of being repatriated. (Verity et al., 2020): "We obtain an overall IFR estimate for China of 0.66% (0.39%,1.33%)".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an epidemiological modeling study (Verity et al., 2020).

claim: The IFR estimates from Verity et al. have been adjusted to account for a non-uniform attack rate giving an overall IFR of 0.9% (95% credible interval 0.4–1.4%).
source: (Ferguson et al., 2020): "The IFR estimates from Verity et al. have been adjusted to account for a non-uniform attack rate giving an overall IFR of 0.9% (95% credible interval 0.4–1.4%)".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an epidemiological modeling study (Ferguson et al., 2020).

claim: The infection fatality risk (IFR) is 0.3% to 0.6% based on repatriation data.
source: (Nishiura et al., 2020): "The infection fatality risk (IFR) – the actual risk of death among all infected individuals – is therefore 0.3% to 0.6%".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an epidemiological study (Nishiura et al., 2020).

claim: The all-age cIFR on the Diamond Princess was estimated to be 1.3% (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.38–3.6).
source: The second approach relies on data gathered from the Diamond Princess ship, where all passengers were tested. (Russell et al., 2020): "We estimated that the all-age cIFR on the Diamond Princess was 1.3% (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.38–3.6)".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an epidemiological study (Russell et al., 2020).

claim: The most recent crude infection fatality ratio (IFR) is estimated to be 0.04% (95% CrI: 0.03–0.06%) and time-delay adjusted IFR is estimated to be 0.12% (95%CrI: 0.08–0.17%).
source: The third approach relies on epidemiological modeling of case time-series from China. (Mizumoto et al., 2020): "We also found that most recent crude infection fatality ratio (IFR) and time-delay adjusted IFR is estimated to be 0.04% (95% CrI: 0.03–0.06%) and 0.12% (95%CrI: 0.08–0.17%)".
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an epidemiological modeling study (Mizumoto et al., 2020).

claim: The crude estimated range for the infection fatality rate (IFR) of SARS-CoV-2 is approximately 0.3–1.3%.
source: Combining these three methods, and taking into account the reliability of each report, we estimate a crude range of ≈0.3–1.3% for the IFR.
evidence: This is an inference based on combining multiple IFR estimates from different studies.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is primed by TMPRSS2.
source: primed by TMPRSS2
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1.
